title: ART gathers govt, business leaders to close super gap
full_text:
The Australian Retirement Trust (ART) is working with the government and business leaders to address the gender superannuation gap.
The forum brings together senior leaders from the Queensland government, ART, Chief Executive Women, Business Chamber Queensland, Financial Basics Foundation, and the Public Sector Commission to explore practical ways to improve women's long-term financial knowledge, participation and leadership.
ART chief executive Kathy Vincent said improving retirement outcomes for women would require action across every stage of working life.
"At Australian Retirement Trust, we see firsthand how career breaks, caring responsibilities, lower lifetime earnings and unequal opportunities can compound over time and contribute to a gender super gap," Vincent said.
"Women are retiring with significantly less super than men, and we believe that should change.
"We're proud to support conversations that bring together employers, government and industry leaders to help more women retire with confidence, security and choice."
ART data has shown women continue to retire with average superannuation balances around 23% lower than men at 60 years. This follows careers in which women are more likely than men to work part-time, represent 67% of primary carers, and on average earn less than men.
On average, women retire with about $50,000 less than men in their superannuation, according to the Super Members' Council.
Minister for women and women's economic security Fiona Simpson said women had reported that economic security included having the freedom and confidence to make choices about their future.
"While Queensland women are making significant progress, many continue to face lower superannuation balances, lower financial confidence and barriers that affect long-term financial outcomes," Simpson said.
"The women's economic security strategy is designed to create the right conditions for women to build their own success, and today's discussion is another important step in that journey."
Business Chamber Queensland chief executive Heidi Cooper said its recent The Future of Women in Business Report highlighted both the progress being made and the work still ahead.
"Queensland women are not simply participating in our economy. They are building it," Cooper said.
"Removing unnecessary barriers to women's entrepreneurship is not only good for individual business owners, it will also strengthen Queensland's overall business ecosystem and support greater economic activity across the state."
